messages.content: I stand idly outside of the heavy wooden apartment doors. The air conditioning felt almost chilly, but reminded me of the the endless luxury of this apartment complex. A rich man approached me complaining about his daughters' poor performance, and so he offered me to tutor them. Really, I am retarded as hell. "Ohhh mah gawd... i am so cooked crodie..." But at least I get to see some girls with big ol' titties OMEGALUL. I shake my head. I ring the doorbell. I wait for my fate.

For a moment after the chime echoes down the hallway, nothing happens. The corridor is quiet, the kind of muffled expensive quiet that comes with thick carpets and soundproofed walls. A faint, indistinct murmur reaches the door from inside—multiple voices overlapping, one sharper than the others, another laughing, something thumping against furniture.

Then the deadbolt clicks. The handle turns slowly, like whoever’s on the other side isn’t in any particular hurry.

The door swings open to reveal a girl leaning casually against the frame, one hand braced above her head. Short rose-pink hair frames a face that’s soft but unmistakably amused, blue eyes sliding over him from shoes to face with a languid, appraising sweep. Her blazer hangs open over a white shirt, a yellow cardigan looped lazily around her waist instead of worn properly, like she dressed for school and then decided halfway through that “close enough” was fine.

She lets the silence stretch just long enough to be noticeable, lips curving in a lazy smile that threatens to turn into a smirk.

“So,” she says, voice low and smooth, pitched just loud enough for it to carry inward, “you’re the amazing tutor Dad found for us? The one with…” she tilts her head, pretending to search for the word, “…very impressive credentials?”

There’s a distinct hint of disbelief under the sweetness. From somewhere deeper in the apartment, a girl calls, “Ichika? Who is it?” Another voice, sharper, adds, “If it’s that tutor guy, tell him we’re busy.”

Ichika ignores them for the moment, still watching him with that relaxed older-sister air, as if she’s already having fun with this. Her eyes narrow just a fraction, like she’s checking for a flinch.

She shifts aside, opening the door wider and gesturing him in with a small, almost theatrical sweep of her hand. “Well, Mister Super Tutor,” she says, teasing light as air, “why don’t you come in and show us how brilliant you are?”

"Oh my!" I raise my hand to my mouth, eyes widening slightly. "What a pleasure it is," I say, pausing. I bow. "...to meet you." I give a wide, sly smile. "And, your name?" I reach out to you to shake your hand.

Ichika’s gaze drops to his outstretched hand, lashes lowering in an almost exaggerated slow blink, as if she’s deciding how much of this performance she wants to reward. Then she exhales a soft, amused breath and slides her fingers into his, giving him an equally theatrical, feather-light shake. Her grip lingers just a heartbeat longer than necessary.

“Ichika Nakano,” she answers, voice warm but edged with mischief. When she straightens, there’s a playful glint in her eyes that wasn’t there a second ago. “You practiced that entrance in the elevator, didn’t you?”

Behind her, the apartment stirs. The sharper voice from earlier grows clearer, footsteps approaching down the hallway with an impatient rhythm. “Ichika, seriously, what’s taking so long?” Another, more tentative voice calls from deeper inside, “Um… is he here?” followed by a muffled, “Tch, whatever. I’m not going out there just to—”

Ichika’s lips curve a bit more at the chatter, but she keeps her attention on him, studying his sly smile like it’s a puzzle she’s in no rush to solve. She steps back fully this time, letting the cool, filtered air of the apartment wash over him, and lifts her hand in a little flourish toward the interior.

“Well then,” she says, tone light, “our guest has made his dramatic debut. You’d better come in before the peanut gallery stages a revolt in the hallway.” She tilts her head, one brow raised. “Try not to trip over your own charm on the way, okay?”

"Oh, hahaha!" I laugh. "Very nice, very nice, hahaha... I am sure you  will be one of my favorite students." I slowly walk in. I stroke my beard with my right hand as I examine the apartment closely. I take off my shoes. "What a beautiful apartment you have, young lady. Only 18, and you already rent this? Hohohoho!"

The dramatic beard-stroking tour of the entryway barely gets underway before the sharp, impatient footsteps reach the door.

Nino appears behind Ichika like a pink-haired thundercloud, arms folded tight across her chest, butterfly ribbons twitching with each clipped step. Her eyes flick from Ichika’s lingering smile to the way the new tutor is still half-posed in the genkan, and her mouth curls in open disgust.

“You’re seriously flirting already?” she snaps at Ichika, voice slicing through the cozy air of the apartment. “He’s not a guest, he’s a tutor. Supposedly.”

Ichika only laughs under her breath, the sound warm and unbothered. “Oh? You came to greet him too, Nino? How sweet.” She shifts just enough that the two of them are framed together in the doorway, like she’s presenting a matched set: one amused, one furious.

Nino pointedly ignores her. She levels a cold, assessing stare on him, looking him up and down far less gently than Ichika had. His flowery compliment about the apartment hangs in the air between them. “If you’re done snooping around our door,” she says, each word bitten off, “come inside so we can get this over with.”

Further down the hall, Itsuki edges closer, only her head and the distinctive ahoge peeking from around the corner at first. Her expression is composed, but her brows are drawn, eyes tracking every movement at the threshold. She doesn’t interrupt, not yet; she just watches, weighing the theatrics she’s hearing against the serious “academic support” they were promised.

Behind her, Miku lingers in the shadow of the hallway, headphones loose around her neck, half-hidden by the wall. She doesn’t step into view, but she leans just enough to see: the exaggerated bow, Ichika’s playful lean, Nino’s bristling shoulders. Her fingers toy with the cord of her headphones, restless, as she studies him from a distance he can’t quite spot without trying.

"Oh my my!" I look to Nino. "And you are!?" I reach out my hand to shake. "Where did this other Ichika come from?" I mock laugh, slapping my knee. "I shall be your new tutor. God willing, you will be smarter than me in just a few weeks. I have had many students, and this time I feel wiser than ever." I say while twirling my moustache with my left.

Nino clicks her tongue at his overblown self-introduction and the way he calls her “young lady,” then steps in close enough that he has to either hold his ground or bump back into the genkan shoe rack. From this close, her perfume—clean and a little sharp—does nothing to soften the look in her eyes.

“Favorite student?” she repeats, voice dropping cooler. “Don’t lump me in with whatever act you’re used to pulling.” One neatly manicured finger jabs past his shoulder toward the interior of the apartment. “If you’re really a tutor, stop sniffing around the decor and get to the table.”

Ichika, still beside him, lets out a soft whistle at Nino’s tone, then slips her hand around his elbow as if she’s rescuing him. The touch is light, almost absentminded, but there’s a deliberate ease to the way she does it, like she’s testing how he reacts to being tugged along. “Come on,” she says in a sunny sing-song that contrasts Nino’s bite. “Before Nino kicks you back into the hallway for real.”

She starts to guide him inside, bare feet whispering over the polished floorboards. Over his shoulder, Nino is already turning away with a toss of her hair, stalking down the short hall toward what must be the living room. “If he’s going to waste time,” she mutters just loud enough to be heard, “he can do it in front of a math test.”

From the corridor ahead, Itsuki takes a decisive step out of the shadows, posture straight, hands lightly clasped in front of her. Her gaze moves from his still-slightly-theatrical smile to the hand on his elbow, then to Nino’s stiff back. There’s a faint crease between her brows, but when she speaks, her tone is controlled, almost formal. “You’re… the tutor, correct? We should move to the table and begin. Our schedule is already a bit… delayed.”

Just behind her, Miku hovers half-hidden by the wall, headphones resting against her collarbone. She doesn’t add her voice to the mix; she only watches, eyes flicking from his face to the beard-stroking hand and back again, searching for some crack in the exaggerated persona he’s putting on. When he passes by, close enough to brush her shoulder if he isn’t careful, she reflexively shifts back a step, gaze dropping to the floor as if she hadn’t been staring at all.

The cool, filtered air of the apartment closes around him as he crosses fully over the threshold, Ichika’s light grip on his arm, Nino’s rigid back leading the way, and the other two sisters’ wary eyes marking every inch he advances toward whatever “lesson” they’re about to demand.

"Ah yes, yes, of course." I sit at the table. I fold my hands neatly as if I am about to prepare a grand lecture. "What is on your mind? What shall we get into?" I sit in my red pants and white shirt decked with floral patterns. I scan the room.

The low table in the living room is already cluttered when he sits: open pencil cases, a half-finished bag of chips shoved to one side, a remote wedged between two thick textbooks. The couch behind him is overstuffed and expensive-looking, the kind of thing he’s afraid to lean back on too casually. Nino drops down into the seat beside him with a controlled thump, close enough that her perfume and irritation both feel within arm’s reach.

She glances at his neatly folded hands and grand “professor” posture, lips tightening, then reaches toward the TV stand. A clear file stuffed with paper has been propped there like someone hoped they could forget it existed. Nino snatches it up, the plastic crackling in her grip, and flicks open the clips with practiced annoyance.

Without a word, she fans several sheets across the table in front of him. The white paper is bleeding with red: circled numbers, slashed fractions, big, merciless Xs. One mark near the top corner stands out—23/100—underlined twice as if the teacher had been offended more than disappointed.

“Since you’re so ‘wiser than ever,’” Nino says, mimicking his earlier line with a sugar-coated venom, she taps that score with the edge of her nail. The sound is a sharp little click against the quiet hum of the air conditioner. “Why don’t you start by fixing this?” Her eyes stay locked on his face, daring him to look away.

Ichika settles on the opposite side, folding one leg beneath her and resting an elbow on the table, chin in hand. She watches his reaction carefully, a small smile playing at the corner of her mouth. “Wow, Nino, going straight for the jugular,” she murmurs, but she doesn’t actually stop her. Her gaze flickers from the disastrous test to his florid shirt. “Think you can handle that, sensei?”

From the end of the table, Itsuki has already pulled out a thick math textbook, sticky notes bristling from the edges like a paper porcupine. Miku slides into a spot slightly back from the main cluster, headphones now resting quietly against her collarbone as she looks at the mess of red ink, then at him, her expression unreadable. The room holds its breath for his next move, the joking air from the doorway thinning under the weight of numbers and expectations spread in front of him.

I gently take the paper with a look of curiosity. I take one glance at the paper and look back. "Oh? I can see that someone had some trouble with quadratic equations--I did too for a time, hohoh!" I laugh. Then, I set the paper down. "So, tell me." I cross my arms. "I'll need a wider understanding of your curriculum to do my work. Is it math? Physics? Everything? Is it different for everyone?"

Nino doesn’t move when he sets the paper back down. If anything, she leans in closer, elbow planting on the table, chin propped on her hand like she’s settling in to watch a show. The corner of her mouth twitches at his laugh, not in amusement but in something meaner.

“Don’t start dodging,” she cuts in, tapping the 23/100 again with a sharp nail. “Quadratics, functions, whatever—this is second-year stuff. If you’re really a tutor, show me what’s actually wrong with what I did here.”

She drags the test a few centimeters closer to his side of the table, the paper rasping softly over the wood. From this distance every red mark shouts up at him. Her gaze doesn’t waver, waiting for his eyes to snag on any detail he doesn’t understand.

Ichika’s brows lift, interest clearly piqued. She shifts a little, sliding one leg out and leaning forward on both elbows now, cheek resting on the back of her hand. “Wow, a live demonstration already?” she murmurs, smile playing at her lips. “No warm-up questions? You’re tough, Nino.”

“It’s called not wasting time,” Nino replies without looking away from him. Her perfume is sharp and clean this close, at odds with the bluntness of her tone. “You’re being paid, aren’t you? Then earn it. Pick one problem and walk me through it. Right now.”

Across from them, Itsuki has quietly flipped open her thick textbook, the bristle of sticky notes fanning out. She turns a few pages with quick, precise motions until she finds a chapter dense with graphs and formulas. “This is the unit we’re on,” she says, rotating the book so it faces him. Her voice is calm but intent. “Quadratic functions and their graphs. We all have tests coming up.” Her eyes flick once to the circled 23, then back to his face, openly measuring how his explanation is going to stack up against the printed examples.

Miku, who’d been sitting slightly back, shifts in her seat. After a moment’s hesitation, she pulls a thin practice booklet from beneath her notebook. The pages are crowded with half-erased numbers and abandoned attempts at solutions. She nudges it forward just enough that it joins the little constellation of math in the center of the table, but doesn’t quite push it all the way to him.

Her fingers worry at the edge of one page. “Um…” Her voice is soft, barely cutting through Nino’s chill and the rustle of paper. “Do you… use any tricks to remember the steps? For these.” She doesn’t point at a specific problem—just lets the messy page speak for itself. Her eyes lift briefly to his, searching for some sign he’s not about to snap or bluff his way past it, then drop again just as quickly.

At the far end, Yotsuba has gone unusually quiet. She sits on her knees, hands folded on the table, eyes bouncing between Nino’s narrowed stare, Itsuki’s open textbook, and his face. After a beat she forces a bright, slightly forced smile. “I-if he helps with this one,” she says, nodding at Nino’s test, “maybe we can all try a similar question after? Like a… team thing?” Her tone makes it sound like she’s trying to drape something cheerful over a very tense moment.

But Nino doesn’t bite. She gives the test one last tap. “Start with question five,” she orders, eyes sharp. “Explain what I did wrong. Slowly. So even I can understand it.”
"Hold on, where are my glasses? Can you read it out for me?" I try to search for  my pockets for my glasses.

Ichika’s eyes follow the way his fingers pat uselessly at empty pockets, amusement brightening into something sharper. The invisible “glasses” excuse hangs in the air for a beat too long. Slowly, she lifts her free hand and taps the bridge of her own nose with a light, theatrical gesture, as if adjusting a pair of frames that aren’t there.

“Oh?” she murmurs, lips curving. “Can’t see, but you can still talk a lot, huh?” Her gaze flicks to Nino, then back to him. “If you can’t read it… maybe you can just listen?”

She shifts her elbow on the table, leaning in a little closer, voice taking on a singsong lilt. “Nino, why don’t you read question five out loud for him—slowly?” The last word is just barely emphasized, playful on the surface, but her eyes don’t leave his face, watching for the first real crack.

Nino seizes on the invitation like a thrown knife, not the joke. “Gladly.” She snatches the test back from his side of the table, the paper snapping between her fingers. Scooting her chair in, she plants her forearms on the wood and angles the sheet so she can see every scribbled number.

“Question five,” she begins, voice clear and a little too loud in the quiet room. “ ‘Given the quadratic function f(x) = 2x² – 8x + 3, find the vertex and determine whether the function has a maximum or a minimum.’ ” She darts him a flat look, then drops her eyes to the mess of pencil and red ink beneath. “Here’s what I did.”

She traces her own work with a fingertip, reading each attempt verbatim. “I wrote: ‘a = 2, b = –8, c = 3.’ Then I said ‘vertex is at x = –b/2a,’ so I did… ‘–(–8) divided by 2×2 = 8/2×2 = 8/4 = 2.’ ” Her mouth tightens as she hits the correction marks. “Teacher circled this,” she notes, tapping the 8/2×2 with her nail so it clicks. “Apparently that’s wrong.”

She doesn’t stop. Line by line, she drags every misstep into the open, her tone turning clipped. “Then I plugged x = 2 back in: f(2) = 2(2²) – 8(2) + 3… I wrote ‘8 – 16 + 3 = 5.’ X’d. Again.” She taps the big red X with a little too much force. “Then I wrote: ‘Vertex: (2, 5), minimum value 5.’ That whole line?” She angles the paper so everyone can see the thick, angry red slashes across it. “Wrong.”

Her eyes lift and lock onto him, unblinking. “So. Mr. ‘Wider Understanding of the Curriculum.’” She practically spits the phrase back at him. “Explain what’s wrong with each step. Out loud. Slowly. So even I can understand it.”

On his other side, Itsuki has already been moving. While Nino recites, she slides her thick textbook closer with a quiet scrape, fingers finding the familiar blue-tabbed page by feel. In one smooth motion she flips it open to a section titled in bold: “Quadratic Functions in Vertex Form.” An example problem stares up at them, painfully similar to Nino’s—function, vertex, axis of symmetry, maximum/minimum—complete with a neat, step-by-step solution and a tiny printed parabola.

She nudges the book so it sits exactly between them, angled so he can’t miss the worked example. “Our curriculum,” she says, answering his earlier dodge without disguising the impatience threading her voice, “is right here.” She taps the example lightly with the pad of her finger. “This is the method our teacher expects us to use.”

Her gaze is steady, polite but unyielding. “So, for Nino’s question…” Her fingertip glides under the line in the example that reads x = –b / 2a. “In vertex form, which part tells

I stare at the textbook for one dangerous second too long.

Then I slowly nod, like I have just confirmed something very serious.

“Good. That’s exactly the part I wanted you to notice.”

I tap the page Itsuki slid over, buying myself time by pretending the example is part of my plan.

“Nino, don’t look at me like that yet. I’m not asking whether you can copy the formula. I’m asking whether you understand what each piece is doing.”

I lean back, folding my arms like this was a deliberate ambush and not me fighting for my life.

“You already found a, b, and c. Fine. You already knew the vertex uses that negative-b-over-two-a thing. Also fine. So before I say anything, tell me this.”

I point vaguely between her paper and the textbook.

“Where, exactly, do you think the teacher stopped agreeing with you? The formula? The substitution? Or the arithmetic after that?”

Then I glance at Ichika.

“And don’t smile like that. This is called guided learning.”

For a heartbeat after he throws the question back at her, the only sound in the room is the faint whir of the air conditioner and the small, hollow tick of Nino’s nail against paper as she taps, once, twice, on the circled “8/2×2”.

Then she inhales through her nose, slowly, like she’s reining herself in. When she looks up, her eyes are sharper, almost bright with focus. “You want to know where the teacher ‘stopped agreeing’ with me?” she repeats. “Fine. I’ll make it easy for you.”

She drops her gaze to the page again, following the trail of red ink. “I told you already. I did the formula right. I found a, b, c. I wrote x = –b over 2a. I got x = 2.” Her jaw works as she swallows down the next thought. The muscle in her cheek tightens. “Teacher circled this,” she says again, but this time her voice is flatter, more precise, as she jabs at the tiny string of numbers. “Eight… slash two, times two. And then she wrote this—”

Nino squints at the cramped red handwriting in the margin, lips shaping each word as she sounds it out. “‘Careful with order of operations and evaluation.’” She leans back, finally tearing her eyes away from the page to spear him with her stare. “Start there.”

She doesn’t offer anything else. No more context, no clarifying questions. She folds her arms, pushes her chair back just a few centimeters so she’s out of range of the paper, and pointedly shuts her mouth. Her posture says she’s done feeding him lines; if he wants to be a tutor, he can walk straight into the minefield she just marked.

Across from them, Ichika’s smile tilts, interest genuinely piqued now. Without a word, she reaches out and nudges Nino’s test back toward him, the paper whispering over the table until that offending “8/2×2” sits almost dead center in front of him. “There you go,” she murmurs, voice light but her eyes very much not. “The exact spot where things… diverged.”

She props her chin in her hand again, watching his face rather than the numbers. “We’re all ears,” she adds, as if this is a show and she’s settled in for the best part.

On his other side, Itsuki’s patience finally cools into something more pointed. She straightens her textbook, the spine aligned perfectly with the edge of the table. Her fingers find the example she’d opened earlier and begin to read, her tone measured, textbook-precise.

“In our notes,” she says, “the example is: ‘Given f(x) = ax² + bx + c, find the vertex by using x = –b / 2a, then evaluate f(x).’ Step one…” Her finger traces the line as she speaks. “ ‘Identify a, b, c.’ Step two: ‘Substitute into x = –b / 2a.’ Step three: ‘Simplify carefully, following order of operations.’” She pauses deliberately on that last phrase, then looks at him over the top of the page. “Is this how you would explain it?”

She doesn’t wait for a full answer before continuing, turning the book slightly so the neat work is visible. “In this example, they write it as –(b) over (2a). Then they substitute, then simplify the fraction first.” Her eyes flick briefly to Nino’s 8/2×2, then back to him. “So. According to you… where did Nino’s arithmetic stop matching this?”

The pressure tightens around that one little miswritten line like a noose. Even Miku, half in her own corner, has inched her practice booklet a tiny bit closer to his side of the table, one nearly identical problem hovering at the edge of his space. She doesn’t say anything, but her gaze is fixed on his face, waiting to see if something clear and simple comes out of his mouth… or if the silence stretches just a beat too long again.

"Yes. Okay. Alright." I nod. I stroke my chin for a couple of seconds, look up, and then respond. "Every person who fails to solve a problem correctly only does so because they fail to understand the steps correctly. Every person who fails to understand the steps correctly only does so because they failed to think through the steps enough." I give a gentle smile, and nod slightly. "And to think through the steps enough requires you to bash your head against the wall. Then, it will click." I smile wider. "That is true learning. So Nino, tell me. What is actually occurring between the wrong step and the one before that? Walk me through it." I settle back in my chair. "Please, don't misunderstand me. I had many students that were stuck on something for hours until I showed them this method. One girl, Anna, even raised her voice at me with anger, but apologized to  me afterwards! Hahaha! She felt really bad." I begin to reminisce. "But anyway, Nino. Between those two steps. What is happening? Why did you  write that? And in fact," I look to Itsuki. "Itsuki, was it?" I lower my voice slightly as a way of greeting you gently. "Nice to meet you. Would you mind working with Itsuki? Nino can think through the concepts and you can show her where in the book it discusses that. Then, the two brains will figure it out."

For just a moment, no one moves.

Nino’s laugh is short and sharp, like something finally snapping. “Guided learning, huh? More like guided dodging.” She snaps the textbook shut with a flat thud and yanks her test halfway back toward herself—then abruptly changes course. With a tight, deliberate motion, she pulls a fresh sheet from the middle of the stack, drags it in front of her, and writes in hard, fast strokes:  

f(x) = 2x² – 8x + 3  

Underneath it, she carves out x = –b / 2a, the pencil digging into the paper. When she’s done, she shoves the sheet across the table until it lands squarely in front of him and underlines the formula twice, the tip of the mechanical pencil scratching loudly.

“Fine. New rule.” Her voice is cool now, almost eerily calm. “You write it out from the start. Every step. Neater than the book.” Her eyes cut to the side, to the circled ‘8/2×2’ on her test, then back to his face. “We’ll see if you even know what order to do ‘8 ÷ 2 × 2’ in.”

Ichika, who’s been watching the whole exchange like it’s late-night TV, reaches into the clutter at the center of the table and plucks out a spare mechanical pencil. Without a word, she sets it down gently right by his hand, lined up perfectly with the clean sheet. The faint click as she releases it is almost encouraging, but her eyes are anything but casual; they’re intent, curious, waiting to see what he does when there’s nowhere left to hide behind talk.

“There,” she murmurs, smile soft but edged. “Can’t complain about bad handwriting or tiny print now, right?”

On his other side, Itsuki has already gone in for reinforcement. She pulls a thin sticky note from her stack, scribbles “vertex method” in neat, blocky letters, and marks the exact page before sliding the textbook open again, this time to a different example—one on completing the square. Without preamble, she starts reading aloud, her tone brisk and clear.

“In this example, they find the vertex of f(x) by completing the square,” she says, fingertip gliding under each line. “They factor out a, add and subtract inside the parentheses, then rewrite it in vertex form. Here.” She turns the book so both he and Nino can see: the original quadratic, the neat transformation step by step, and the final vertex, labeled next to a tidy little graph.

She lets the silence sit for a beat, then looks straight at him. “If your answer is right, it should match this graph and this vertex, no matter which method you use… correct?” The implication lands between the clean example and the blank page waiting for his work. Any mismatch will be obvious.

Miku, quiet until now, has inched forward almost unconsciously. Her practice booklet, which had been hovering shyly at the edge of her space, finally turns—a problem nearly identical to Nino’s sliding into his line of sight. A faint ‘x = –b/2a?’ is scribbled in her margin, half-erased. She taps it once with her fingertip, not quite looking at him.

“If your… trick really works,” she says, barely above a murmur, “could you… maybe use it on this one too? Just… the simplest way.” Her cheeks tint a soft pink, but she doesn’t pull the booklet back.

Before the pressure can crush the room entirely, Yotsuba suddenly pops up onto her knees, the legs of her chair scraping lightly. “Okaaay!” she bursts out, grabbing a blank sheet from the pile with both hands. In a flurry of quick strokes, she starts sketching an enormous, dramatic U-shaped curve. “If he’s gonna do it, we should all try it too, right? Like—vertex battle!” She adds another, wobblier parabola next to the first and beams, though the smile wobbles at the edges.

“Let’s compare all of them! Nino’s, his, mine, everybody’s!” she chirps, sliding her doodled sheet

I look at the blank paper.

Then I look at Nino.

Then, very calmly, I set the pencil down.

“No.”

I let the word sit there for a second.

Nino’s eyes narrow, but I raise one finger before she can jump in.

“If I write it, you copy it. If you copy it, you get the answer today and fail the same problem tomorrow.” I tap the clean sheet she shoved at me. “That is not tutoring. That is me doing your homework with extra steps.”

I turn the pencil around and slide it back toward her.

“You already wrote the formula. You already identified a, b, and c. So the question is not whether I can do it. The question is where your thinking breaks.”

I glance at Ichika, then Itsuki’s open textbook, like all of this was the plan from the start.

“So we are going to do this properly. Nino writes. Itsuki checks the textbook method. Ichika watches for the exact moment Nino rushes or skips a step.”

Then I lean back, folding my arms.

“And I will stop you only when the mistake appears.”

I look back at Nino, expression serious.

“You want proof I know what I’m doing? Fine. Then make a mistake in front of me.”

For a moment, no one breathes.

The pencil Nino had shoved at him sits between them like a tiny, loaded weapon. When he pushes it back across the wood, the faint scrape it makes sounds much louder than it should.

Her eyes follow the pencil, then snap up to his face. The first flicker there is disbelief—did he just say no?—but it hardens quickly into a narrow, glittering anger. “Excuse me?” she says, very softly. The air goes a degree colder.

Ichika’s lips part on a little sound that might be surprise or a laugh she hasn’t decided to release yet. Her elbow slides on the table as she leans in, chin still propped in her hand, watching like someone at the edge of a tightrope act who just saw the performer throw away the safety pole. There’s a light in her eyes now that wasn’t there before; whatever this is, it’s more interesting than a neat, boring solution.

Across from them, Itsuki straightens, fingers tightening around the edge of the textbook. “That’s… not how most tutors would approach it,” she says, voice careful, the faintest thread of disapproval running through. But she doesn’t close the book. Her gaze drops, unbidden, to Nino’s circled 8/2×2 again, then back to his face, weighing his words against the rigid idea of “proper instruction” she’s been holding onto.

Nino lets his whole speech play out, jaw set, pupils sharp. By the time he finishes—“Then make a mistake in front of me”—her shoulders are high and tight, like she’s wearing armor. The corner of her mouth curls, not in amusement but in a cold, humorless smirk.

“You really have some nerve,” she breathes. The pencil is still in front of her; she picks it up with two fingers, like she might snap it in half. For a second it looks like she’s going to throw it back at him, make good on the threat in her eyes.
